keyVerseText: In the third year of the reign of king Belshazzar a vision appeared unto me, even unto me Daniel, after that which appeared unto me at the first.
rootMeaning: The name בֵּלְשַׁאצַּר (Bêlshaʼtstsar) is of foreign origin and means "Bel protect the king." This reflects a theophoric element invoking the Babylonian deity Bel, emphasizing divine protection over the monarch. The root name connects closely to בֵּלְטְשַׁאצַּר (Bêlṭᵉshaʼtstsar), meaning "lord of the straitened's treasure," which was Daniel's Babylonian name. Together, these names highlight a cultural context where royal authority was seen as under divine safeguarding and stewardship of resources.
usageInScripture: The term בֵּלְשַׁאצַּר appears only once in Scripture, specifically in Daniel 8:1, where it is translated consistently as "Belshazzar." This singular occurrence associates the name directly with a Babylonian king during the empire's decline, to whom Daniel had significant prophetic visions and interpretations. The consistent translation underscores the historical and narrative focus on this figure as a key ruler in the biblical account of Babylon's fall.
theologicalSignificance: Understanding the original meaning of בֵּלְשַׁאצַּר as "Bel protect the king" deepens our awareness of the tension between earthly and divine authority in Scripture. While the name invokes protection by a Babylonian god, the biblical narrative reveals that true sovereignty belongs to the God of Israel, who ultimately judges kings and kingdoms. This contrast invites believers to trust in God's ultimate reign and justice rather than in human or pagan powers. Belshazzar's role as a king whose fate was interpreted by Daniel points to God's providential control over history and His revelation to His faithful servants.
keyVerseReflection: Daniel 8:1 states, "In the third year of the reign of king Belshazzar a vision appeared unto me, even unto me Daniel, after that which appeared unto me at the first." The use of בֵּלְשַׁאצַּר here situates the vision historically under the authority of this Babylonian king, emphasizing the real-world context of divine revelation. The name's meaning, "Bel protect the king," contrasts with the unfolding vision, reminding readers that God's purposes transcend human rulers and their supposed divine protection.
